mock.note: 25 multiple choice questions like Smartgrade. Then answer one 5 mark and one 12 mark question from the Written practice tab.

units.name: Islam: Sunni and Shi'a and the key beliefs
Islam: angels, predestination, life after death
Peace, justice, forgiveness, protest and terrorism
Reasons for war and the just war theory

group_labels.P: Theme D: Religion, peace and conflict

leitner_plan.new: Sunni and Shi'a, nature of Allah (7)

cards.title: Sunni and Shi'a: how the split began
cards.question: Why did Islam divide into Sunni and Shi'a Muslims?
points: The Prophet Muhammad died in 632 CE. Muslims disagreed about who should lead the community next.
Sunni Muslims accepted Abu Bakr, the Prophet's close friend, chosen by the community, as the first caliph.
Shi'a Muslims believe the Prophet chose Ali, his cousin and son in law, and that leadership should stay in his family.
Sunni Muslims are the large majority (around 85 to 90%) of Muslims worldwide.
cards.watch_out: Both groups share the same core beliefs, the Qur'an and the Five Pillars. The split is mainly about leadership, not about God.
cards.hook: Shi'a comes from Shi'at Ali, the party of Ali.
cards.grade9: Explain why the split still matters: Shi'a Muslims follow Imams who they believe are guided by God, which shapes their authority.

cards.title: The Six Articles of Faith (Sunni)
cards.question: What are the Six Articles of Faith in Sunni Islam?
points: Tawhid: belief in one God (Allah).
Malaikah: belief in angels.
Kutub: belief in the holy books.
Risalah: belief in the prophets.
Akhirah: belief in the Day of Judgement and life after death.
Al-Qadr: belief in predestination, that Allah knows and decides everything.
cards.watch_out: The Six Articles are beliefs. The Five Pillars are actions (practices). Do not mix them up.
cards.hook: Tall Men Keep Running After Quails: Tawhid, Malaikah, Kutub, Risalah, Akhirah, Qadr.
cards.grade9: Link each article to how it affects a Muslim's life, for example Akhirah encourages good behaviour because of judgement.

cards.title: The Five Roots of Usul ad-Din (Shi'a)
cards.question: What are the five roots of Usul ad-Din in Shi'a Islam?
points: Tawhid: the oneness of God.
Adalat: God's justice. God is fair and will judge fairly.
Nubuwwah: prophethood, belief in the prophets.
Imamah: belief in the twelve Imams as leaders chosen by God, starting with Ali.
Mi'ad: the Day of Judgement and resurrection.
cards.watch_out: Imamah and Adalat are the roots that most clearly differ from the Sunni Articles of Faith.
cards.hook: TANIM: Tawhid, Adalat, Nubuwwah, Imamah, Mi'ad.
cards.grade9: Compare: both include Tawhid, prophethood and judgement; Shi'a add justice and the Imamate as separate roots.

cards.title: Tawhid: the oneness of Allah
cards.question: What is Tawhid and why is it the most important belief in Islam?
points: Tawhid means Allah is one, unique and indivisible. Nothing shares His power or nature.
Surah 112 teaches that Allah is one and eternal, has no parents or children, and nothing is comparable to Him.
Shirk is the sin of associating anything with Allah. It is the most serious sin.
This is why there are no images of Allah or the Prophet in mosques; art uses geometric patterns and calligraphy.
cards.watch_out: Do not say Muslims worship Muhammad. He is a prophet and a human being; only Allah is worshipped.
cards.grade9: Use Surah 112 as your sacred writing reference in 5 mark answers on the nature of Allah.

cards.title: Omnipotence, beneficence and mercy
cards.question: What do Muslims believe about Allah's power, goodness and mercy?
points: Omnipotent: all powerful. Allah created the universe and controls everything.
Beneficent: all loving and kind. Allah provides everything humans need.
Merciful: Allah forgives those who are truly sorry. Almost every surah begins In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful.
These qualities are among the 99 names of Allah.
cards.watch_out: If asked for a teaching, the opening words of the surahs (the Bismillah) are an easy, accurate reference for mercy.
cards.grade9: Discuss the problem of evil: if Allah is all powerful and merciful, why is there suffering? Muslims may see it as a test.

cards.title: Justice, immanence and transcendence
cards.question: What do Muslims mean by Allah being just, immanent and transcendent?
points: Fairness and justice (Adalat): Allah treats everyone fairly and will judge everyone on the Day of Judgement.
Immanent: Allah is close to and involved in the world. The Qur'an says Allah is closer to a person than their jugular vein.
Transcendent: Allah is beyond and outside the world, time and human understanding.
Muslims believe Allah is both at once: beyond understanding, yet close.
cards.watch_out: Immanent (close, inside the world) and imminent (about to happen) are different words. Spell immanent with an a.
cards.hook: Immanent is in the world; transcendent transcends (goes beyond) it.
cards.grade9: Evaluate the tension: how can Allah be both close and beyond us? Muslims answer that Allah is not limited, so both are possible.

cards.title: Free will versus a just God
cards.question: Why is Allah's justice important for free will?
points: If Allah is just, it is fair to judge people only if they freely chose their actions.
Shi'a Muslims stress Adalat: God gave humans free will so judgement is fair.
Sunni Muslims stress al-Qadr: Allah knows and has written everything, but humans are still responsible.
Most Muslims say: Allah knows what we will choose, but we still choose.
cards.watch_out: Predestination does not mean Muslims believe they can do nothing. They are still accountable for their actions.
cards.grade9: Use the analogy that knowing what someone will choose does not force their choice.

cards.title: Risalah: the role of prophets
cards.question: What is Risalah, and why are Adam and Ibrahim important?
points: Risalah means prophethood: Allah sends messengers to guide humans. Muslims believe there were many prophets.
Adam was the first prophet and first human, made from clay. Allah taught him the names of things; he was given free will and later repented.
Ibrahim (Abraham) rejected idol worship and taught belief in one God. He rebuilt the Ka'aba in Makkah with his son Isma'il.
Ibrahim was willing to sacrifice his son, showing complete submission to Allah (remembered at Id ul-Adha).
cards.watch_out: Prophets are human, not divine. Muslims show respect by saying peace be upon him after their names.
cards.hook: A, I, M: Adam first, Ibrahim the friend of God, Muhammad last.
cards.grade9: Link prophets to practice: Hajj and Id ul-Adha remember Ibrahim, so beliefs shape worship.

cards.title: Muhammad, the Seal of the Prophets
cards.question: Why is Muhammad the most important prophet in Islam?
points: Muhammad is the final prophet, the Seal of the Prophets. No prophet comes after him.
In 610 CE, on the Night of Power, the angel Jibril brought the first revelation in the cave on Mount Hira.
Revelations continued for about 23 years and became the Qur'an.
He set up the first Muslim community in Madinah after the Hijrah (migration) in 622 CE; his example is the Sunnah.
cards.watch_out: Muhammad did not write the Qur'an. Muslims believe it is the direct word of Allah, revealed through Jibril.
cards.grade9: Explain why being the final prophet matters: his message completes and corrects earlier revelations.

cards.title: The holy books (Kutub)
cards.question: Which holy books do Muslims believe in, and why is the Qur'an the highest authority?
points: The Qur'an: the final, complete and unchanged word of Allah, revealed to Muhammad in Arabic.
Earlier books: the Tawrat (Torah) to Musa, the Zabur (Psalms) to Dawud, the Injil (Gospel) to Isa, and the Scrolls (Suhuf) of Ibrahim.
Muslims believe the earlier books were changed or lost over time, so the Qur'an has supreme authority.
The Qur'an is treated with great respect: kept clean, handled after washing, recited in Arabic.
cards.watch_out: The Injil was given to Isa (Jesus). Muslims respect Jesus as a prophet but not as the Son of God.
cards.hook: Tawrat to Musa, Zabur to Dawud, Injil to Isa: T, Z, I before Q.
cards.grade9: Explain why recitation in Arabic matters: translations are seen as interpretations, not the Qur'an itself.

cards.title: Angels (Malaikah)
cards.question: What are angels in Islam and what do Jibril and Mika'il do?
points: Angels are made from light, have no free will and always obey Allah.
Jibril (Gabriel) brought Allah's revelation to the prophets, including the Qur'an to Muhammad.
Mika'il (Michael) is the angel of mercy, who provides rain and nourishment.
Other angels record every person's deeds and will play roles on the Day of Judgement, such as Israfil blowing the trumpet.
cards.watch_out: Humans have free will; angels do not. This is a common 1 or 2 mark question.
cards.grade9: Explain how belief in recording angels affects behaviour: Muslims know every action is written down for judgement.

cards.title: Al-Qadr: predestination
cards.question: What is al-Qadr, and how does it fit with free will?
points: Al-Qadr means Allah has decided and knows everything that will happen.
Muslims may say insha'Allah (if God wills) when they talk about the future.
Humans still have free will and are responsible for their choices; this makes judgement fair.
Sunni Muslims give al-Qadr greater emphasis; Shi'a Muslims stress that Allah's justice requires free will.
cards.watch_out: Do not write that Muslims believe in fate so nothing matters. Al-Qadr encourages trust in Allah, not laziness.
cards.hook: Insha'Allah: the everyday reminder of al-Qadr.
cards.grade9: Offer two views: predestination comforts people in hard times, but some argue it makes judgement seem unfair.

cards.title: Akhirah: life after death
cards.question: What do Muslims believe happens after death?
points: After death the soul waits in Barzakh until the Day of Judgement.
On the Day of Judgement everyone is resurrected and judged by Allah on their beliefs and deeds.
Those judged good enter Jannah (paradise), described as a garden; those judged bad go to Jahannam (hell).
Belief in Akhirah gives life meaning and encourages responsibility and accountability.
cards.watch_out: Muslims believe Allah's mercy matters on the Day of Judgement too, so judgement is not only a list of good and bad deeds.
cards.grade9: Link Akhirah to everyday behaviour (charity, prayer, honesty) to answer how this belief influences Muslims.

cards.title: Peace, justice, forgiveness and reconciliation
cards.question: What do these key terms mean, and what do Christians and Muslims teach about them?
points: Peace: an absence of conflict, and harmony between people. Justice: fairness, where everyone is treated equally.
Forgiveness: showing mercy and pardoning someone. Reconciliation: restoring friendly relationships after conflict.
Christianity: Jesus taught Blessed are the peacemakers (Matthew 5:9) and to love your enemies.
Islam: the word Islam is linked to salam (peace). Muslims greet each other with As-salamu alaykum (peace be upon you). Justice is a key duty.
cards.watch_out: Peace is not only the absence of war. Both religions say there can be no lasting peace without justice.
cards.grade9: Use a real example of reconciliation, such as Coventry Cathedral's ministry of reconciliation after the Second World War.

cards.title: Violent protest and terrorism
cards.question: What do Christians and Muslims believe about protest, violent protest and terrorism?
points: Protest: expressing disapproval, often in public. Peaceful protest is legal in the UK and supported by both religions.
Most Christians and Muslims oppose violent protest because it harms innocent people. Martin Luther King used non violent protest.
Terrorism: the use of violence and threats to intimidate, often for political purposes.
Both religions condemn terrorism. The Qur'an teaches that killing an innocent person is like killing all of humanity.
cards.watch_out: Do not suggest terrorists represent a religion. Religious leaders of both faiths condemn terrorism as a misuse of religion.
cards.grade9: Evaluate: some argue violent protest can be justified against great injustice, but religious teachings usually prefer peaceful means.

cards.title: Reasons for war
cards.question: What are the main reasons for war, and what do religions say about them?
points: Greed: to gain land, resources such as oil, or power. Both religions condemn war for greed.
Self defence: protecting your country or people. Most Christians and Muslims accept this as a valid reason.
Retaliation: hitting back after an attack. Jesus taught turn the other cheek; the Qur'an allows fighting back but not beyond limits.
Other causes: religion, ideology, protecting others from injustice.
cards.watch_out: Retaliation and self defence are not the same. Retaliation is revenge after the attack; self defence is protecting yourself during it.
cards.grade9: Give a contrasting view within one religion, such as Christian pacifists (Quakers) who reject all reasons for war.

cards.title: The just war theory
cards.question: What are the conditions of the just war theory?
points: Developed by Christian thinkers, especially St Thomas Aquinas, from ideas of St Augustine.
Just cause: for example self defence or to correct a wrong.
Correct authority: declared by a proper authority, such as a government.
Right intention: to promote good and stop evil, not for greed or revenge.
Last resort, reasonable chance of success, and proportional: the force used should not be greater than the harm it prevents, and civilians must be protected.
cards.watch_out: All the conditions must be met for a war to be just, not just one.
cards.hook: CARL CP: Cause, Authority, Right intention, Last resort, Chance of success, Proportion.
cards.grade9: Evaluate with modern weapons: can a nuclear war ever be proportional or protect civilians?

cards.title: Islamic teaching on war
cards.question: What are the Islamic conditions for a justified war (lesser jihad)?
points: Greater jihad is the inner struggle to live as a good Muslim. Lesser jihad is the outer struggle, including a just war.
It must be declared by a proper religious authority and fought in self defence or to protect Islam or the oppressed.
It must be a last resort and not for land, power or revenge.
Civilians, crops, animals and religious buildings must not be harmed, and fighting stops when the enemy asks for peace.
The Qur'an allows fighting those who fight you but warns not to overstep the limits (Surah 2:190).
cards.watch_out: Jihad does not simply mean holy war. Most Muslims see the greater jihad (personal struggle) as more important.
cards.grade9: Compare with the Christian just war theory: both require proper authority, a just cause and protection of civilians.

cards.title: Christian views on war and pacifism
cards.question: What range of views do Christians have about war?
points: Many Christians accept the just war theory: war can be a necessary evil in some cases.
Romans 13 teaches Christians to respect governing authorities, which some use to support serving in the armed forces.
Pacifists, such as Quakers, refuse to take part in any war. They follow Jesus' teaching to love your enemies.
Jesus said those who take up the sword will die by the sword (Matthew 26:52).
cards.watch_out: Pacifists are not passive. Many work actively for peace, for example through aid and campaigning.
cards.grade9: For 12 mark answers, show the range: just war Christians, pacifist Christians, and Muslims who follow lesser jihad rules.

cards.title: 1, 2 and 4 mark questions
cards.question: How do you answer the short AQA RS questions?
points: 1 mark: multiple choice. Read all four options before choosing.
2 marks: name two or give two. Short, clear answers; no explanation needed.
4 marks: explain two ways or two contrasting beliefs. For each: make a point, then develop it with an explanation (2 + 2).
Contrasting means different views, either between religions or within one (Sunni and Shi'a, just war and pacifist).
cards.watch_out: In a 4 mark contrasting question, two similar beliefs only score half the marks.
cards.grade9: Use key terms (Tawhid, Adalat, lesser jihad) in your development to show precise knowledge.

cards.title: 5 and 12 mark questions
cards.question: How do you answer the 5 mark and 12 mark questions?
points: 5 marks: explain two beliefs (point and development each), plus one reference to sacred writing or another source of religious belief.
12 marks: evaluate a statement. Give arguments for and against, with religious reasons, then reach a justified conclusion.
12 mark plan: for (two developed reasons), against (two developed reasons), conclusion that weighs them up.
Refer to religious teachings and say which arguments are stronger and why.
cards.watch_out: A 12 mark answer without religious arguments cannot reach the top level, however good the opinions are.
cards.hook: 5 mark: two beliefs plus a book. 12 mark: for, against, judge.
cards.grade9: Evaluate each argument as you go: This is a strong argument because ..., but it is weaker because ...

cards.title: Key quotes and teachings
cards.question: Which teachings can you use as sacred writing references?
points: Surah 112: Allah is one and eternal; nothing is comparable to Him (Tawhid).
Opening of the surahs: In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful (mercy).
Qur'an: Allah is closer than the jugular vein (immanence). Surah 2:190: fight those who fight you, but do not go beyond the limits.
Matthew 5:9: Blessed are the peacemakers. Matthew 5:44: Love your enemies. Matthew 26:52: those who take the sword die by the sword.
Qur'an 5:32: killing one innocent person is like killing all of humanity.
cards.watch_out: A paraphrase of a teaching is fine. Say where it comes from, such as the Qur'an or Matthew's Gospel.

written.q: Explain two Muslim beliefs about the nature of Allah. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Muslim belief and teaching in your answer.
model: First belief, such as Tawhid: Allah is one and unique (1)
Development: so Muslims reject shirk and do not make images of Allah (1)
Second belief, such as immanence: Allah is close to and involved in the world (1)
Development: Muslims believe Allah hears every prayer (1)
Relevant source, such as Surah 112 or Allah is closer than the jugular vein (1)

written.q: Explain two contrasting beliefs about who should have led the Muslim community after the death of Muhammad.
model: Sunni Muslims believe the community chose Abu Bakr (1)
Development: he was a close friend of the Prophet, chosen as the best person to lead (1)
Shi'a Muslims believe Muhammad chose Ali (1)
Development: leadership should stay in the Prophet's family through the Imams (1)

written.q: Explain two ways in which belief in life after death influences Muslims today.
model: Muslims try to live good lives and follow the Five Pillars (1)
Development: because they will be judged on their deeds on the Day of Judgement (1)
Muslims may give to charity and help others (1)
Development: recording angels write down every action, so they are accountable (1)

written.q: War can never be justified. Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should give reasoned arguments to support this statement, give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view, refer to religious arguments and reach a justified conclusion.
model: For: pacifist Christians such as Quakers follow Jesus' teaching to love your enemies (2)
For: war kills innocent civilians and modern weapons cannot be proportional (2)
Against: the just war theory says war can be justified with just cause, correct authority and last resort (2)
Against: Islam allows lesser jihad in self defence, Surah 2:190, with strict rules (2)
Evaluation of the strength of each side, using key terms (2)
Justified conclusion that follows from the arguments (2)

written.q: Explain two religious beliefs about the conditions needed for a war to be just. Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
model: It must be a last resort after all peaceful methods have failed (1)
Development: because life is sacred and war causes suffering (1)
It must be declared by a proper authority (1)
Development: for example a government in Christianity, or a religious leader for lesser jihad (1)
Relevant source, such as Aquinas, Romans 13 or Surah 2:190 (1)

exam_tips.timing: 30 minutes writing: about 3 minutes for a 4 mark, 5 for a 5 mark, 12 to 15 for a 12 mark. 20 minutes Smartgrade.
section_a: Smartgrade questions test key terms. Learn the Arabic words and their meanings exactly.
Read all four options before choosing.
section_b: 4 and 5 marks are point, develop, point, develop. 5 marks add a source.
12 marks need for, against, religious arguments and a conclusion.
Name the religion and the group (Sunni, Shi'a, Quaker, Catholic) when you give a view.
grade9: For 5 mark questions name the source of authority, such as the Qur'an teaches. A quotation with no source can cost the fifth mark.
Explain how a belief changes what a believer does. Belief in judgement leads to taking responsibility for actions.
Define the disputed term first. Lesser jihad means a just struggle with strict rules, not any war.
After each argument in a 12 mark answer say why it is stronger or weaker, then reach a reasoned conclusion.
Show diversity within a religion, not only between religions.
Use accurate key terms throughout; spelling counts on 12 mark questions.

mcq.q: In which year did the Prophet Muhammad die?
mcq.e: 570 birth, 610 first revelation, 622 Hijrah, 632 death.

mcq.q: Who do Sunni Muslims accept as the first caliph?
mcq.e: He was chosen by the community.

mcq.q: Who do Shi'a Muslims believe should have led after Muhammad?
mcq.e: Ali was the Prophet's cousin and son in law.

mcq.q: Which is NOT one of the Six Articles of Faith?
mcq.e: Zakah (charity) is one of the Five Pillars, which are practices.

mcq.q: Which root of Usul ad-Din means God's justice?
mcq.e: Adalat is justice.

mcq.q: Which root is about belief in the twelve Imams?
mcq.e: Imamah is the Shi'a belief in the Imams as God chosen leaders.

mcq.q: Roughly what proportion of Muslims are Sunni?
mcq.e: Sunni Muslims are the large majority.

mcq.q: What does Tawhid mean?
mcq.e: Tawhid is the central belief of Islam.

mcq.q: What is shirk?
mcq.e: Shirk is the most serious sin.

mcq.q: Which surah is a key teaching on Tawhid?
mcq.e: It teaches Allah is one, eternal and unique.

mcq.q: What does omnipotent mean?
mcq.e: Omni means all; potent means powerful.

mcq.q: What does immanent mean?
mcq.a: Close to and involved in the world
mcq.e: Allah is closer than the jugular vein.

mcq.q: What does transcendent mean?
mcq.e: Transcendent means going beyond.

mcq.q: Why are there no pictures of Allah in mosques?
mcq.a: Allah is unique and nothing can represent Him
mcq.e: Images could lead to shirk.

mcq.q: Who was the first prophet in Islam?
mcq.e: Adam was the first human and first prophet.

mcq.q: Which prophet rebuilt the Ka'aba with his son?
mcq.e: Ibrahim and Isma'il rebuilt the Ka'aba.

mcq.q: What is meant by the Seal of the Prophets?
mcq.e: No prophet comes after Muhammad.

mcq.q: Where did Muhammad receive the first revelation?
mcq.e: On the Night of Power in 610 CE.

mcq.q: To which prophet was the Injil (Gospel) given?
mcq.e: The Tawrat went to Musa, the Zabur to Dawud.

mcq.q: Why does the Qur'an have the highest authority for Muslims?
mcq.a: It is the final, unchanged word of Allah
w: It is the oldest holy book
mcq.e: Earlier books are believed to have been changed.

mcq.q: What are angels made from in Islam?
mcq.e: Humans are made from clay; jinn from fire.

mcq.q: Which angel brought the revelation of the Qur'an?
mcq.e: Jibril is the angel of revelation.

mcq.q: Which angel provides rain and nourishment?
mcq.e: Mika'il is linked to mercy and provision.

mcq.q: What is al-Qadr?
mcq.a: Predestination: Allah knows and decides everything
mcq.e: Qadr means power or decree.

mcq.q: What do Muslims mean by insha'Allah?
mcq.e: It reflects belief in al-Qadr.

mcq.q: What is Barzakh?
mcq.a: The waiting state between death and the Day of Judgement
mcq.e: The soul waits in Barzakh.

mcq.q: What is Jannah?
mcq.e: Jahannam is hell.

mcq.q: What is reconciliation?
mcq.e: It often follows forgiveness.

mcq.q: Which teaching is from Matthew 5:9?
mcq.e: Part of the Sermon on the Mount.

mcq.q: Which Arabic word, linked to Islam, means peace?
mcq.e: As-salamu alaykum means peace be upon you.

mcq.q: What is terrorism?
mcq.a: Using violence and threats to intimidate, often for political aims
mcq.e: Both religions condemn it.

mcq.q: Which Qur'an teaching is used to condemn terrorism?
mcq.a: Killing one innocent person is like killing all humanity
w: Allah is closer than the jugular vein
There is no compulsion in religion
mcq.e: Surah 5:32.

mcq.q: Which is NOT a just war condition?
mcq.e: Fighting for land is greed, which is never just.

mcq.q: Which thinker developed the just war theory?
mcq.e: Building on ideas from St Augustine.

mcq.q: What is retaliation?
mcq.a: Fighting back in revenge for an attack
mcq.e: Jesus taught turn the other cheek.

mcq.q: What is the greater jihad?
mcq.a: The inner struggle to live as a good Muslim
mcq.e: Lesser jihad is the outer struggle, including just war.

mcq.q: According to Islamic teaching, when must fighting stop?
mcq.a: When the enemy asks for peace
mcq.e: Surah 2 teaches that if they cease, fighting stops.

mcq.q: Which Christian group is known for pacifism?
mcq.e: Quakers refuse to fight in any war.

mcq.q: What does proportional mean in the just war theory?
mcq.a: Force must not cause more harm than it prevents
w: Both sides must have equal weapons
mcq.e: Excessive force makes a war unjust.

mcq.q: How many marks is the evaluation question worth?
mcq.e: It asks you to evaluate a statement.

mcq.q: What does a 5 mark question need that a 4 mark question does not?
mcq.a: A reference to sacred writing or a source of religious belief
mcq.e: Two developed beliefs plus a source.

mcq.q: In a 4 mark contrasting question, what must your two points be?
mcq.e: Contrasting means different views.

vocab.example: In Islam, monotheism is expressed in the belief called Tawhid.

vocab.meaning: God making something known to humans
vocab.example: The first revelation came to Muhammad in 610 CE.
Muslims believe Allah is omnipotent and created everything.

vocab.meaning: Present and active within the world
vocab.example: Allah is immanent because He is closer than the jugular vein.

vocab.meaning: Beyond and outside the world and time
vocab.example: A transcendent God cannot be pictured or fully understood.

vocab.meaning: The belief that God has already decided what will happen
vocab.example: Belief in predestination is called al-Qadr.

vocab.meaning: Being responsible for your actions and having to answer for them
vocab.example: Belief in judgement gives Muslims a sense of accountability.

vocab.meaning: The belief that all violence and war is wrong
vocab.example: Quakers are known for their pacifism.
After the war, the cathedral became a centre of reconciliation.
Jesus taught that retaliation is wrong.
